questions.q: Which country was the main rival of the United States during the Cold War?
questions.explain: The Cold War was a decades-long rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, from the late 1940s until the Soviet collapse in 1991.

questions.q: Why is the U.S.-Soviet rivalry from the late 1940s to 1991 called the "Cold" War?
options: It was fought mostly in Arctic regions
It took place only during winter months
It was fought entirely at sea
The two powers never fought each other directly
questions.explain: The superpowers competed through alliances, arms, and proxy wars, but never fought a full-scale war directly against each other.

questions.q: Which president told the Soviet leader in a 1987 Berlin speech, "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!"?
questions.explain: Ronald Reagan spoke at the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin on June 12, 1987. The wall fell two years later.

questions.q: In what year did the Soviet Union break apart into separate countries?
questions.explain: The Soviet Union formally dissolved in December 1991, ending the Cold War and leaving the United States as the only superpower.

questions.q: Who was the leader of the Soviet Union when it broke apart in 1991?
questions.explain: Mikhail Gorbachev led the Soviet Union from 1985 and resigned on December 25, 1991, as the country dissolved.

questions.q: East and West Germany reunited as a single country in what year?
questions.explain: German reunification took place on October 3, 1990, less than a year after the Berlin Wall opened.

questions.q: What military alliance did the United States, Canada, and Western European nations form in 1949?
questions.explain: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) was founded in 1949; its members pledged to defend one another against attack.

questions.q: What did the Marshall Plan do after World War II?
options: Set up the United Nations in New York
Gave U.S. aid to rebuild Western Europe
Paid Japan to give up its colonies
questions.explain: Under the Marshall Plan (1948-1952) the U.S. sent about 13 billion dollars to help rebuild Western European economies and resist communism.

questions.q: During the Cold War, the U.S. policy of "containment" aimed to do what?
options: Reduce the size of the Navy
questions.explain: Containment, adopted under President Truman, sought to keep communism from spreading to new countries.

questions.q: Which British leader warned in a 1946 speech that an "iron curtain" had fallen across Europe?
questions.explain: Winston Churchill gave the "Iron Curtain" speech in Fulton, Missouri, in March 1946, describing the split between communist East and democratic West.

questions.q: During the 1948-1949 Berlin Airlift, how did the U.S. and Britain get supplies to West Berlin?
questions.explain: When the Soviets blocked roads and rail lines into West Berlin, Western planes flew in food and coal for about 11 months until the blockade ended.

questions.q: Senator Joseph McCarthy became famous in the early 1950s for doing what?
options: Leading troops in the Korean War
questions.explain: McCarthy claimed communists had infiltrated the government; "McCarthyism" now means reckless accusations of disloyalty. The Senate censured him in 1954.

questions.q: The Cold War "arms race" was mainly a competition to build more of what?
questions.explain: The U.S. and the Soviet Union built tens of thousands of nuclear warheads, each side trying to match or outpace the other.

questions.q: Which president led the United States during the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962?
questions.explain: In October 1962 Kennedy ordered a naval "quarantine" after Soviet missiles were found nearby; the Soviets agreed to remove them.

questions.q: The failed 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion tried to overthrow the government of which country?
questions.explain: CIA-trained Cuban exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs in April 1961 to overthrow Fidel Castro, but they were quickly defeated.

questions.q: In 1957 the Soviet Union shocked Americans by launching the first artificial satellite. What was it called?
questions.explain: Sputnik 1 orbited Earth in October 1957 and kicked off the space race. The U.S. answered with Explorer 1 in 1958.

questions.q: The Korean War began in June 1950 when North Korea invaded which country?
questions.explain: North Korean forces crossed into South Korea on June 25, 1950. The United States and United Nations sent troops to defend the South.

questions.q: Which president sent U.S. troops to fight in Korea in 1950?
questions.explain: Harry Truman committed U.S. forces under a United Nations command days after North Korea invaded the South.

questions.q: How did the shooting in Korea come to a stop in 1953?
options: With a U.S. victory that united Korea
With China taking over the whole peninsula
With an armistice that left Korea divided
With a peace treaty signed in Tokyo
questions.explain: An armistice signed in July 1953 stopped the fighting near the 38th parallel. No formal peace treaty has ever been signed.

questions.q: Korea was divided into North and South near which line of latitude?
questions.explain: Korea was split at the 38th parallel after World War II, and the 1953 armistice line runs close to it. (Vietnam was later split at the 17th.)

questions.q: The Korean War Veterans Memorial on the National Mall shows a squad of soldier statues doing what?
options: Raising a flag on a hilltop
Walking on patrol through a field
questions.explain: Nineteen stainless-steel soldiers in ponchos move through juniper bushes, as if on patrol. The flag-raising statue is the Marine Corps War Memorial.

questions.q: Which famous U.S. general commanded United Nations forces early in the Korean War until Truman removed him in 1951?
questions.explain: Truman relieved Douglas MacArthur in April 1951 after MacArthur publicly challenged the president's war policy.

questions.q: The United States fought in the Vietnam War mainly to stop the spread of what?
questions.explain: U.S. leaders feared that if South Vietnam fell to communism, other countries in Southeast Asia would follow, the so-called domino theory.

questions.q: Who was the communist leader of North Vietnam during much of the Vietnam War?
questions.explain: Ho Chi Minh led North Vietnam until his death in 1969; Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City after the war.

questions.q: What is carved into the black granite walls of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial?
options: The full text of the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution
A map of the battles of the Vietnam War
The names of Americans who died or went missing
Quotations from the presidents who led the war
questions.explain: The wall lists more than 58,000 names of service members who died or remain missing, arranged in the order they were lost.

questions.q: The Vietnam Veterans Memorial was designed by Maya Lin when she was what?
questions.explain: Maya Lin was a 21-year-old Yale architecture student when her design won a national competition in 1981.

questions.q: Which president sharply increased the number of U.S. troops in Vietnam after the 1964 Gulf of Tonkin Resolution?
questions.explain: Lyndon Johnson used the resolution to escalate the war; U.S. troop levels rose to over 500,000 by 1968.

questions.q: The Tet Offensive of 1968 was a large surprise attack carried out by whom?
options: U.S. Marines and South Korean troops
North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces
questions.explain: Communist forces struck cities across South Vietnam in January 1968. Though pushed back, the attack turned many Americans against the war.

questions.q: Under which president did the last U.S. combat troops leave Vietnam in 1973?
questions.explain: After the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973, Richard Nixon withdrew the remaining U.S. combat forces by March 1973.

questions.q: In 1970, Ohio National Guard troops fired on college students at Kent State University who were protesting what?
questions.explain: On May 4, 1970, guardsmen killed four students during protests against the U.S. invasion of Cambodia, part of the Vietnam War.

questions.q: In what year did Saigon fall to North Vietnam, ending the Vietnam War?
questions.explain: North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon on April 30, 1975, as the last Americans were evacuated by helicopter.

questions.q: In which Alabama city did Rosa Parks refuse to give up her bus seat in 1955?
questions.explain: Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery on December 1, 1955, sparking the year-long Montgomery bus boycott.

questions.q: Rosa Parks was arrested in 1955 for refusing to give up her seat on what?
questions.explain: Parks would not give her seat on a Montgomery city bus to a white passenger. Her arrest led to a boycott and a court ruling against bus segregation.

questions.q: The Supreme Court's 1954 ruling in Brown v. Board of Education declared what unconstitutional?
options: Prayer led by teachers in schools
questions.explain: Brown v. Board overturned "separate but equal" in public education, ruling that segregated schools violate the 14th Amendment.

questions.q: Who was the first Black justice on the U.S. Supreme Court?
questions.explain: Thurgood Marshall, who had argued Brown v. Board of Education, joined the Court in 1967 after President Johnson nominated him.

questions.q: In what year did Martin Luther King Jr. give his "I Have a Dream" speech?
questions.explain: King spoke on August 28, 1963, at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.

questions.q: In which city did Martin Luther King Jr. deliver his "I Have a Dream" speech?
questions.explain: About 250,000 people gathered on the National Mall for the 1963 March on Washington, where King spoke from the Lincoln Memorial steps.

questions.q: Martin Luther King Jr. led civil rights protests using what approach?
questions.explain: Inspired partly by Gandhi, King urged peaceful marches, boycotts, and sit-ins, even in the face of violence.

questions.q: In 1957, which president sent federal troops to protect the Little Rock Nine as they entered a white high school?
questions.explain: Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne Division to Little Rock, Arkansas, to enforce school desegregation at Central High School.

questions.q: In the 1960 Greensboro sit-ins, Black college students protested segregation at what kind of place?
questions.explain: Four students sat at a whites-only Woolworth lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina; part of that counter is now at the Smithsonian.

questions.q: In 1947, Jackie Robinson broke Major League Baseball's color barrier playing for which team?
questions.explain: Robinson debuted with the Brooklyn Dodgers on April 15, 1947. Every MLB team now retires his number 42.

questions.q: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlaw?
options: Child labor in factories and mines
Discrimination based on race, religion, or sex
questions.explain: The act banned job discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, and outlawed segregation in public places such as hotels and restaurants.

questions.q: The 1965 marches from Selma to Montgomery, Alabama, demanded what?
options: An end to the Vietnam War
questions.explain: Violence against marchers on "Bloody Sunday" shocked the nation and helped pass the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

questions.q: The statue of Martin Luther King Jr. at his DC memorial appears to emerge from what?
questions.explain: King's figure is carved into the "Stone of Hope," inspired by his line about hewing a stone of hope out of a mountain of despair.

questions.q: The national holiday honoring Dr. King falls in which month each year?
questions.explain: The holiday falls on the third Monday in January, near King's birthday of January 15. It was first observed nationally in 1986.

questions.q: Which month is celebrated as Black History Month in the United States?
questions.explain: February was chosen because it contains the birthdays of Abraham Lincoln and Frederick Douglass. Presidents have recognized it since 1976.

questions.q: Title IX, passed in 1972, is best known for expanding school sports for whom?
questions.explain: Title IX bans sex discrimination in schools that receive federal money, which opened many more athletic opportunities for female students.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to serve on the Supreme Court?
questions.explain: Ronald Reagan appointed Sandra Day O'Connor in 1981. She served until 2006.

questions.q: Who became the first Hispanic justice on the Supreme Court, in 2009?
questions.explain: Sonia Sotomayor, a judge from New York of Puerto Rican descent, was nominated by Barack Obama and confirmed in 2009.

questions.q: Who became the first Black woman to serve on the Supreme Court, in 2022?
questions.explain: Ketanji Brown Jackson was confirmed in April 2022 and sworn in that June, replacing Justice Stephen Breyer.

questions.q: Which president signed the Voting Rights Act of 1965?
questions.explain: Lyndon Johnson signed the act on August 6, 1965. It suspended literacy tests and other tricks used to keep Black citizens from voting.

questions.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
questions.explain: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon on July 20, 1969; Buzz Aldrin followed while Michael Collins orbited above.

questions.q: In what year did American astronauts first land on the Moon?
questions.explain: Apollo 11 landed on July 20, 1969, meeting President Kennedy's goal of a Moon landing before the decade was out.

questions.q: Which NASA mission first landed people on the Moon?
questions.explain: Apollo 11 carried Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins. Its command module, Columbia, is displayed at the National Air and Space Museum.

questions.q: Neil Armstrong called his first step on the Moon "one small step for man, one giant leap for" what?
questions.explain: Armstrong's words were heard live by hundreds of millions of people around the world on July 20, 1969.

questions.q: What happened on NASA's Apollo 13 mission in 1970?
options: It was the first mission to land on the Moon
It carried the first woman into space
An explosion forced the crew to skip the Moon landing
It docked with a Soviet space capsule
questions.explain: An oxygen tank exploded on the way to the Moon. The crew looped around the Moon and returned safely to Earth.

questions.q: What reusable NASA spacecraft first flew in 1981?
questions.explain: The Space Shuttle launched like a rocket and landed like a glider. The fleet flew 135 missions before retiring in 2011.

questions.q: Teacher Christa McAuliffe died when which space shuttle broke apart after launch in 1986?
questions.explain: Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff on January 28, 1986, killing all seven crew members.

questions.q: Since 2000, astronauts from the United States, Russia, and other nations have lived aboard what?
questions.explain: The International Space Station has had people living on it continuously since November 2000.

questions.q: What famous NASA space telescope was launched aboard a space shuttle in 1990?
questions.explain: The Hubble Space Telescope has orbited Earth since 1990. The James Webb Space Telescope launched much later, in 2021.

questions.q: In 1961, President Kennedy set a goal of landing a man on the Moon by when?
options: The end of his first term
questions.explain: Kennedy asked Congress in May 1961 to land a man on the Moon "before this decade is out." Apollo 11 did it in July 1969.

questions.q: In which city was President John F. Kennedy assassinated in 1963?
questions.explain: Kennedy was shot while riding in a motorcade through Dallas, Texas, on November 22, 1963.

questions.q: Who became president after John F. Kennedy was assassinated?
questions.explain: Vice President Lyndon Johnson took the oath of office aboard Air Force One in Dallas hours after Kennedy was killed.

questions.q: Which president said in his inaugural address, "Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country"?
questions.explain: John F. Kennedy spoke those words at his inauguration on January 20, 1961.

questions.q: Which volunteer program that sends Americans to help people in other countries did Kennedy create in 1961?
questions.explain: Kennedy created the Peace Corps by executive order in March 1961. Volunteers work in education, health, and farming abroad.

questions.q: What marks President John F. Kennedy's grave at Arlington National Cemetery?
questions.explain: Jacqueline Kennedy asked for an eternal flame, which was lit at his funeral in November 1963 and still burns today.

questions.q: In 1960, John F. Kennedy became the first president of which faith?
questions.explain: Kennedy was the first Catholic elected president. Presbyterians, Methodists, and Episcopalians had all served before him.

questions.q: Who was arrested for the assassination of President Kennedy?
questions.explain: Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested in Dallas the same day and was himself shot dead by Jack Ruby two days later.

questions.q: Richard Nixon is the only U.S. president to have done what?
questions.explain: Nixon resigned in 1974. Others have been impeached, FDR served four terms, and eight presidents died in office.

questions.q: The Watergate scandal is named after what?
options: An office and apartment complex in Washington
A dam the government secretly built
A gate on the White House grounds
A nickname for a secret CIA plan
questions.explain: The scandal began with a June 1972 break-in at Democratic National Committee offices in the Watergate complex beside the Potomac.

questions.q: Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein investigated the Watergate scandal as reporters for which newspaper?
questions.explain: Their reporting for The Washington Post helped expose the cover-up, aided by a secret source nicknamed "Deep Throat."

questions.q: In 1974, the Supreme Court ordered President Nixon to hand over what?
options: Plans for the invasion of Cambodia
Secret tape recordings of White House talks
The names of his campaign donors
questions.explain: In United States v. Nixon the Court ruled unanimously against him. The tapes proved he joined the cover-up, and he resigned weeks later.

questions.q: What did President Gerald Ford do for Richard Nixon in September 1974?
questions.explain: Ford pardoned Nixon for any crimes he may have committed as president, a decision that was very unpopular at the time.

questions.q: In 1972, Richard Nixon became the first sitting president to visit which communist country?
questions.explain: Nixon's trip to China in February 1972 opened relations between the two countries after decades of hostility.

questions.q: Which federal agency that protects the nation's air and water was created in 1970?
questions.explain: The EPA was set up under President Nixon in December 1970 to enforce pollution laws such as the Clean Air Act.

questions.q: What annual event focused on protecting the environment was first held on April 22, 1970?
questions.explain: Some 20 million Americans took part in the first Earth Day, which helped build support for new environmental laws.

questions.q: On September 11, 2001, which building near Washington was struck by a hijacked plane?
questions.explain: American Airlines Flight 77 struck the Pentagon, killing 184 people on the plane and in the building. A memorial now stands at the site.

questions.q: After passengers fought back, hijacked United Flight 93 crashed in a field in which state on September 11, 2001?
questions.explain: Flight 93 went down near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. It is believed the hijackers were aiming for a target in Washington, DC.

questions.q: Who was president of the United States on September 11, 2001?
questions.explain: George W. Bush had taken office in January 2001. He was visiting a school in Florida when the attacks began.

questions.q: In October 2001, the United States began a war in which country, where al-Qaeda leaders were based?
questions.explain: U.S. forces invaded Afghanistan to topple the Taliban, who sheltered al-Qaeda. The last U.S. troops left in August 2021.

questions.q: Which new cabinet department was created in 2002 in response to the September 11 attacks?
questions.explain: The Department of Homeland Security combined more than 20 agencies, including the Coast Guard and Secret Service.

questions.q: In 2011, U.S. Navy SEALs killed Osama bin Laden in which country?
questions.explain: Bin Laden was killed in a raid on his compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, on May 2, 2011 (local time).

questions.q: Two hijacked planes struck the twin towers of which New York City complex on September 11, 2001?
questions.explain: Both towers of the World Trade Center collapsed. Nearly 3,000 people died in the attacks that day.

questions.q: In 2003, a U.S.-led coalition invaded which country and removed Saddam Hussein from power?
questions.explain: The Iraq War began in March 2003. Saddam Hussein was captured that December and later executed by the Iraqi government.

questions.q: The 1991 Persian Gulf War drove Iraqi forces out of which country?
questions.explain: Iraq had invaded Kuwait in August 1990. A U.S.-led coalition freed it in Operation Desert Storm in early 1991.

questions.q: Who was the first Black president of the United States?
questions.explain: Barack Obama was elected in 2008 and served two terms, from 2009 to 2017.

questions.q: In what year was Barack Obama first elected president?
questions.explain: Obama won the November 2008 election and took office in January 2009; he was re-elected in 2012.

questions.q: Before becoming president, Barack Obama represented which state in the U.S. Senate?
questions.explain: Obama was born in Hawaii but built his political career in Chicago and served as a U.S. senator from Illinois from 2005 to 2008.

questions.q: Who served as vice president under Barack Obama?
questions.explain: Joe Biden was vice president from 2009 to 2017 and was later elected president himself in 2020.

questions.q: The Affordable Care Act, signed in 2010, dealt mainly with what?
questions.explain: The Affordable Care Act, often called "Obamacare," set up insurance marketplaces and expanded Medicaid.

questions.q: Who became the first woman to serve as vice president of the United States, in 2021?
questions.explain: Kamala Harris took office in January 2021 as the first woman, and first Black and South Asian American, vice president.

questions.q: In 2016, who became the first woman nominated for president by a major political party?
questions.explain: Hillary Clinton won the Democratic nomination in 2016. She won the popular vote but lost the Electoral College.

questions.q: Which World War II general was elected president in 1952?
questions.explain: Eisenhower, who commanded the D-Day invasion, served two terms as president from 1953 to 1961.

questions.q: Which huge road-building program began under President Eisenhower in 1956?
questions.explain: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 funded about 41,000 miles of interstates, reshaping travel and suburbs.

questions.q: Jonas Salk developed a vaccine in the 1950s against which disease?
questions.explain: Salk's polio vaccine was declared safe and effective in 1955, and cases soon plunged from a disease that had paralyzed thousands of children each year.

questions.q: What was the "baby boom" after World War II?
options: A sharp rise in the number of births
A wave of new immigrants from Europe
A rapid growth in factory jobs
questions.explain: About 76 million Americans were born between 1946 and 1964, a generation known as the baby boomers.

questions.q: Which singer became known as the "King of Rock and Roll" in the 1950s?
questions.explain: Elvis Presley's hits and TV appearances made him the biggest star of early rock and roll.

questions.q: Which British band set off "Beatlemania" when it appeared on American television in 1964?
questions.explain: About 73 million people watched the Beatles on The Ed Sullivan Show in February 1964, launching the "British Invasion."

questions.q: The famous 1969 Woodstock festival was a gathering for what?
questions.explain: Some 400,000 people attended the music festival on a farm in Bethel, New York, in August 1969.

questions.q: Medicare, created in 1965, provides health insurance mainly for whom?
questions.explain: Lyndon Johnson signed Medicare into law as part of his Great Society. Medicaid, created the same day, helps people with low incomes.

questions.q: Before entering politics, Ronald Reagan was best known as what?
questions.explain: Reagan acted in dozens of films, then served as governor of California before becoming president in 1981.

questions.q: Which president survived being shot outside a Washington hotel in 1981?
questions.explain: John Hinckley Jr. shot Reagan outside the Washington Hilton on March 30, 1981, just 69 days into his presidency.

questions.q: The 1978 Camp David Accords, brokered by President Jimmy Carter, made peace between Israel and which country?
questions.explain: Carter hosted Egypt's Anwar Sadat and Israel's Menachem Begin at Camp David; the countries signed a peace treaty in 1979.

questions.q: In the hostage crisis that began in 1979, Americans were held at the U.S. embassy in which country?
questions.explain: Iranian students held 52 Americans for 444 days. The hostages were released in January 1981, minutes after Reagan took office.

questions.q: Which president was impeached by the House in 1998 and acquitted by the Senate in 1999?
questions.explain: Bill Clinton was the second president impeached, after Andrew Johnson in 1868. The Senate did not convict him.

questions.q: Hurricane Katrina devastated which American city in 2005?
questions.explain: Levees failed and about 80 percent of New Orleans flooded. More than 1,300 people died across the Gulf Coast.

questions.q: The severe economic downturn that began around 2007 to 2008 is often called what?
questions.explain: Triggered by a housing and banking crisis, the Great Recession was the worst U.S. downturn since the 1930s.

questions.q: Which disease caused a worldwide pandemic that shut down much of American life in 2020?
questions.explain: COVID-19, caused by a new coronavirus, led to closed schools and businesses; vaccines became available starting in December 2020.

questions.q: The 26th Amendment, ratified in 1971, lowered the national voting age to what?
questions.explain: The amendment passed quickly during the Vietnam War, when many argued that people old enough to be drafted should be able to vote.

questions.q: Which two states joined the Union in 1959, bringing the total to 50?
questions.explain: Alaska became the 49th state in January 1959 and Hawaii the 50th in August 1959.

questions.q: What global computer network spread into millions of American homes in the 1990s?
questions.explain: The World Wide Web, opened to the public in the early 1990s, made the internet easy to use for ordinary households.

questions.q: How many branches does the U.S. federal government have?
questions.explain: The Constitution divides power among the legislative branch (Congress), the executive branch (the president), and the judicial branch (the courts).

questions.q: Which branch of government makes the nation's laws?
questions.explain: Congress, made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives, is the legislative branch and writes federal laws.

questions.q: Which branch of government, led by the president, carries out the laws?
questions.explain: The executive branch includes the president, vice president, and federal departments that enforce and carry out laws.

questions.q: The Supreme Court and other federal courts make up which branch of government?
questions.explain: The judicial branch interprets laws and settles disputes about what the law and the Constitution mean.

questions.q: How many members does the U.S. Senate have in total?
questions.explain: Two senators from each of the 50 states makes 100 senators.

questions.q: How many voting members does the U.S. House of Representatives have?
questions.explain: The number of voting House seats has been set at 435 by law since 1913, shared among the states by population after each census.

questions.q: How long is one term for a U.S. president?
questions.explain: Presidents are elected every four years, and the 22nd Amendment limits them to two elected terms.

questions.q: How long is one term for a U.S. senator?
questions.explain: Senators serve six-year terms, and about one-third of the Senate is up for election every two years.

questions.q: How long is one term for a member of the U.S. House of Representatives?
questions.explain: All 435 House seats are up for election every two years, keeping the House close to public opinion.

questions.q: Who has the power to veto a bill passed by Congress?
questions.explain: The president can veto, or reject, a bill. Congress can still pass it into law by overriding the veto.

questions.q: What vote does Congress need in both the House and Senate to override a presidential veto?
questions.explain: Under Article I of the Constitution, a two-thirds vote in each chamber overrides a veto.

questions.q: What is the main job of the U.S. Supreme Court?
options: To decide what the Constitution and laws mean
questions.explain: The Court hears cases and can strike down laws or government actions that it finds violate the Constitution.

questions.q: How many justices sit on the U.S. Supreme Court today?
questions.explain: The Court has had nine justices, one chief justice and eight associate justices, since 1869.

questions.q: How long can a Supreme Court justice serve?
options: For life, unless they retire or are removed
questions.explain: Federal judges hold office "during good behavior," which in practice means for life unless they retire, resign, or are impeached and removed.

questions.q: Which part of Congress must confirm a president's nominee to the Supreme Court?
questions.explain: The president nominates justices, and the Senate holds hearings and votes to confirm or reject them.

questions.q: Who serves as president of the U.S. Senate under the Constitution?
questions.explain: The vice president presides over the Senate and can cast a vote only to break a tie.

questions.q: What is the title of the leader of the House of Representatives?
questions.explain: Members elect the Speaker, who runs the House and is second in line for the presidency after the vice president.

questions.q: Under the Constitution, who is commander in chief of the U.S. armed forces?
options: The chairman of the Joint Chiefs
questions.explain: Article II makes the president commander in chief, keeping the military under civilian control.

questions.q: Which branch of government has the power to declare war?
questions.explain: Article I gives Congress the power to declare war. It has formally done so 11 times, most recently in World War II.

questions.q: What are the first ten amendments to the Constitution called?
questions.explain: The Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791 and protects freedoms such as speech, religion, and a fair trial.

questions.q: In which city was the U.S. Constitution written in 1787?
questions.explain: Delegates met at Independence Hall in Philadelphia. Washington, DC, did not yet exist.

questions.q: Where in Washington can visitors see the original Declaration of Independence on display?
questions.explain: The Declaration, Constitution, and Bill of Rights are displayed together in the Rotunda for the Charters of Freedom at the National Archives.

questions.q: What is the minimum age to be president of the United States?
questions.explain: Article II requires the president to be at least 35, a natural-born citizen, and a U.S. resident for 14 years.

questions.q: If the president dies or leaves office, who becomes president?
questions.explain: The vice president is first in line. Nine vice presidents have taken over this way, most recently Gerald Ford in 1974.

questions.q: After the House impeaches a president, which body holds the trial?
questions.explain: The Senate tries impeachments. Removal requires a two-thirds vote, which has never happened to a president.

questions.q: How many electoral votes does a candidate need to win the presidency?
questions.explain: There are 538 electoral votes in all, so a majority is 270.

questions.q: What is the group of electors that formally chooses the president called?
questions.explain: Each state gets electors equal to its number of senators and representatives; DC gets three.

questions.q: In which month are U.S. presidential elections held?
questions.explain: Federal elections are held on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November.

questions.q: On what date does a newly elected president take office?
questions.explain: The 20th Amendment (1933) moved Inauguration Day from March 4 to January 20.

questions.q: What do the letters "DC" stand for in Washington, DC?
questions.explain: Congress created the District of Columbia as a federal capital that belongs to no state.

questions.q: What is the group of department heads who advise the president called?
questions.explain: The Cabinet includes the vice president and the heads of the executive departments, such as the secretaries of state and the treasury.

questions.q: What are the first three words of the U.S. Constitution?
questions.explain: The Preamble begins "We the People of the United States," showing that the government gets its power from the people.

questions.q: What is called the "supreme law of the land" in the United States?
questions.explain: Article VI says the Constitution, and federal laws and treaties made under it, are the supreme law of the land.

questions.q: How many amendments have been added to the U.S. Constitution?
questions.explain: The 27th, about congressional pay, was ratified in 1992. The first ten form the Bill of Rights.

questions.q: What is the White House?
options: The building of the Supreme Court
The home and office of the president
questions.explain: Every president since John Adams has lived and worked in the White House at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue.

questions.q: What is the street address of the White House?
questions.explain: The White House sits at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, facing Lafayette Square to the north.

questions.q: What is the name of the president's official office in the West Wing of the White House?
questions.explain: The Oval Office was built in 1909 and moved to its present spot in the West Wing in 1934.

questions.q: What happens in the U.S. Capitol building?
questions.explain: The Senate meets in the north wing and the House in the south wing, under the great cast-iron dome.

questions.q: Which president is honored by the memorial with a giant seated marble statue at the west end of the National Mall?
questions.explain: The Lincoln Memorial, dedicated in 1922, holds a 19-foot statue of the 16th president with his Gettysburg Address carved on the wall.

questions.q: Which famous Lincoln speech is carved into the wall of the Lincoln Memorial, alongside his Second Inaugural?
questions.explain: The south wall carries the Gettysburg Address and the north wall his Second Inaugural Address.

questions.q: What shape is the Washington Monument?
questions.explain: The marble obelisk, finished in 1884, rises about 555 feet and is the tallest monument in Washington, DC.

questions.q: Which president is honored by the round, domed memorial on the Tidal Basin, inspired by the Pantheon in Rome?
questions.explain: The Jefferson Memorial opened in 1943, the 200th anniversary of his birth. Its style echoes Monticello and the Pantheon.

questions.q: The famous cherry trees around the Tidal Basin were a 1912 gift from which country?
questions.explain: The mayor of Tokyo gave about 3,000 trees in 1912. Their spring bloom is celebrated each year with the National Cherry Blossom Festival.

questions.q: Which president, honored by a memorial beside the Tidal Basin, was elected four times?
questions.explain: FDR won in 1932, 1936, 1940, and 1944. The 22nd Amendment later limited presidents to two elected terms.

questions.q: The National World War II Memorial stands on the Mall between the Lincoln Memorial and what?
questions.explain: Opened in 2004, it sits at the east end of the Reflecting Pool, between the Lincoln Memorial and the Washington Monument.

questions.q: What is the long, open park in Washington lined with museums and monuments called?
questions.explain: The National Mall stretches about two miles from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial.

questions.q: What words are carved above the front entrance of the Supreme Court building?
questions.explain: The motto appears on the west front of the building, which opened in 1935.

questions.q: Which Washington institution calls itself the largest library in the world?
questions.explain: The Library of Congress holds well over 170 million items, including books, maps, recordings, and manuscripts.

questions.q: The Library of Congress was created mainly to serve whom?
questions.explain: Founded in 1800 for lawmakers, it later became the nation's library and is open to researchers age 16 and older.

questions.q: What is guarded around the clock by soldiers at Arlington National Cemetery?
options: The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
questions.explain: Soldiers have guarded the tomb 24 hours a day since 1937; since 1948 the sentinels have come from the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment.

questions.q: Arlington National Cemetery is located in which state?
questions.explain: The cemetery lies across the Potomac River from Washington, on land that once belonged to Robert E. Lee's family.

questions.q: Which famous flag, which inspired the national anthem, is displayed at the National Museum of American History?
questions.explain: The huge flag flew over Fort McHenry in 1814 and inspired Francis Scott Key to write the poem that became the national anthem.

questions.q: What happened at Ford's Theatre in Washington in April 1865?
options: The Civil War peace was signed
questions.explain: John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln during a play on April 14, 1865. Lincoln died the next morning in a house across the street.

questions.q: The 1903 Wright Flyer, displayed at the National Air and Space Museum, was built by whom?
questions.explain: Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first powered, controlled airplane flights at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903.

questions.q: Which federal department, headquartered next to the White House, manages the nation's money?
questions.explain: The Treasury Department collects taxes, pays the government's bills, and oversees the making of coins and paper money.

questions.q: The back of the five-dollar bill shows which Washington landmark?
questions.explain: The five-dollar bill has Lincoln on the front and the Lincoln Memorial on the back.

questions.q: Which Founding Father, who was never president, is pictured on the $100 bill?
questions.explain: Benjamin Franklin, never a president, has been on the hundred-dollar bill since 1914.

questions.q: Washington National Cathedral is built in what architectural style?
questions.explain: Begun in 1907 and finished in 1990, the cathedral has pointed arches, flying buttresses, and gargoyles in the Gothic style.

questions.q: What is Union Station in Washington, DC?
options: The headquarters of a labor union
questions.explain: Opened in 1907 near the Capitol, Union Station serves Amtrak, commuter trains, and the Metro.

questions.q: Before becoming a famous speaker and writer, Frederick Douglass escaped from what?
questions.explain: Douglass escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838. He spent his last years at Cedar Hill, his home in Washington's Anacostia neighborhood.

questions.q: The National Museum of the American Indian focuses on whom?
options: Immigrants who came through Ellis Island
questions.explain: The Smithsonian museum on the Mall opened in 2004 and presents the history and cultures of Native peoples across the Western Hemisphere.

questions.q: When a leader "lies in state" in the Capitol Rotunda, what happens?
options: They are sworn into a new office
Their portrait is hung in the dome
They give a farewell speech to Congress
Their casket is displayed for the public to honor
questions.explain: Since Henry Clay in 1852, presidents, lawmakers, and other honored Americans have lain in state beneath the Capitol dome.

questions.q: Which Smithsonian museum on the Mall, opened in 2016, tells the story of Black Americans?
options: The National Museum of American History
The National Museum of African American History and Culture
questions.explain: The museum, with its bronze-colored, three-tiered design, opened in September 2016 near the Washington Monument.
